subject: anatomy
title: Scalp, face and facial nerve: high-yield anatomy

steps.tx: The scalp has five layers, remembered as **SCALP**: skin, dense connective tissue, galea aponeurotica, loose areolar tissue and pericranium. The **loose areolar layer** is the danger zone, because infection or blood spreads freely through it and emissary veins carry infection towards the skull and intracranial venous sinuses. The galea aponeurotica links the frontalis and occipitalis muscles, so the frontalis does not attach to bone.

steps.tx: Scalp sensation comes from ten nerves on each side: five in front of the auricle and five behind it. In front, the **supratrochlear**, **supraorbital**, zygomaticotemporal and **auriculotemporal** nerves are sensory, and the temporal branch of the facial nerve is motor. Behind the ear, the great auricular, lesser occipital, greater occipital and third occipital nerves supply the scalp.

In front, the supratrochlear, supraorbital, zygomaticotemporal and auriculotemporal nerves are sensory. The temporal branch of the facial nerve is motor. Behind the ear, the great auricular, lesser occipital, greater occipital and third occipital nerves supply the scalp.

steps.tx: The facial nerve leaves the skull through the **stylomastoid foramen**, not the foramen lacerum, mastoid foramen or optic canal. It has the longest intraosseous course of the cranial nerves and is the most commonly paralysed. Its five terminal branches, temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical, emerge from the parotid gland.

steps.tx: In **Bell palsy**, a lower motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve causes ipsilateral weakness of all facial muscles. The patient cannot close the eye, tears spill over the cheek and saliva dribbles from the corner of the mouth. Lesions proximal to the geniculate ganglion also cause loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, loss of lacrimation and **hyperacusis** from loss of the stapedial reflex. The mastoid segment and stylomastoid level are where the nerve is most vulnerable.
steps.say: In Bell palsy, a lower motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve causes weakness of all facial muscles on one side. The patient cannot close the eye, tears spill over the cheek and saliva dribbles from the corner of the mouth. Lesions proximal to the geniculate ganglion also cause loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, loss of lacrimation and hyperacusis, because the stapedial reflex is lost.

steps.tx: The **cavernous sinus** lies in the middle cranial fossa beside the sphincter-like body of sphenoid. Infection usually spreads from the ethmoid or sphenoid sinuses, or from the danger area of the face via the angular and facial veins and ophthalmic veins. Features include fever, chemosis, proptosis, fixed dilated pupils and cranial nerve III, IV, V and VI palsies. Loss of the jaw jerk is not a feature, because the jaw jerk depends on the mandibular nerve, which does not run in this sinus.
steps.say: The cavernous sinus lies in the middle cranial fossa beside the body of the sphenoid. Infection usually spreads from the ethmoid or sphenoid sinuses, or from the danger area of the face through the angular and facial veins and ophthalmic veins. Features include fever, chemosis, proptosis, fixed dilated pupils and palsies of cranial nerves three, four, five and six. Loss of the jaw jerk is not a feature, because the mandibular nerve does not run in this sinus.

steps.tx: Trigeminal sensation to the face has three divisions: **ophthalmic (V1)**, **maxillary (V2)** and **mandibular (V3)**. The **tip of the nose** is supplied by the external nasal branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve, a branch of V1. The **lower lip** and **buccal mucosa** are supplied by V3. Do not confuse this with motor control: the **buccal branch of the facial nerve** supplies **buccinator**, which is why buccinator is the whistling muscle.
steps.say: Trigeminal sensation to the face has three divisions: ophthalmic, maxillary and mandibular. The tip of the nose is supplied by the external nasal branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve, a branch of the ophthalmic division. The lower lip and buccal mucosa are supplied by the mandibular division. Buccinator, the whistling muscle, is moved by the buccal branch of the facial nerve, not by the trigeminal nerve.
